note.note:
Consult Summary:
- Adult male with new-onset, painless swelling over the left olecranon consistent with olecranon bursitis; started NSAID therapy and blood work arranged to evaluate inflammatory, rheumatologic, infectious, and gout-related causes with safety-net advice and follow-up planned.

History:
- Presenting complaint: Visible swelling over the tip/near tip of the left elbow noticed ~1 week ago.
- Symptom details:
  - Painless or minimally tender; feels “fluid-filled.”
  - Slightly warm to touch; mild tenderness adjacent to the swelling.
  - Full, normal range of motion; able to use the arm normally.
  - No remembered trauma; desk-based job; runs 2–3 times/week.
  - No prior similar episodes.
  - Skin at elbow tip observed as dry.
- Timeline: Noticed ~1 week prior to consult; patient reports it may be feeling a bit better now.
- Exacerbating/relieving factors: None identified.
- Associated symptoms: No specific systemic symptoms discussed (fever/chills not reported).
- Pertinent negatives mentioned: No known family history of rheumatoid arthritis or lupus.

Past Medical History:
- Osteoarthritis: Previously diagnosed by GP (details/site not specified). No complications noted.
- Allergic to peanuts.

Medications:
- Current regular medications: None.
- New recommendation: Ibuprofen 400 mg by mouth twice daily after food; stop if heartburn occurs (duration not specified).
- Allergies:
  - Peanuts (food).
  - No known medication allergies.

Social History:
- Occupation: Desk-based work.
- Activity: Runs 2–3 times per week.
- Tobacco, alcohol, and other substances: Not recorded.

Family History:
- Denies known family history of rheumatoid arthritis or lupus (patient not sure, but reports no).

Physical Examination:
- Vitals: Not recorded.
- Musculoskeletal (video assessment of left elbow):
  - Visible swelling over the olecranon region.
  - Skin slightly warm.
  - Mild tenderness adjacent to swelling; tip itself not very tender.
  - Dry skin over the tip of the elbow noted.
  - Full range of motion preserved.
  - No marked erythema recorded.
- General: Clinician impression—does not look like septic arthritis.

Investigations:
- Ordered/planned:
  - Blood tests to assess inflammatory markers and infection.
  - Rheumatologic antibody screen.
  - Serum urate (gout screen).
- Logistics/timeline:
  - Blood test forms to be mailed to patient with instructions where to attend.
  - Results expected approximately 5–6 days after blood draw.
- Imaging: None mentioned.

Assessment & Plan:
- Overall Impression:
  - Likely non-septic olecranon bursitis of the left elbow. Presentation and exam are not suggestive of septic arthritis at this time. Work-up planned to assess for inflammatory/rheumatologic and crystal etiologies including gout.

- DDx Integration (brief):
  - Aseptic (nonseptic) olecranon bursitis – supported by painless, fluctuant swelling with slight warmth and preserved ROM; no systemic illness; clinician’s impression aligns. Opposes: no explicit repetitive pressure history.
  - Gouty olecranon bursitis – possible given age/sex and acute swelling with warmth; opposes: minimal pain, no prior gout.
  - Septic olecranon bursitis/arthritis – low likelihood now; supported by warmth and dry skin (potential risk); opposes: minimal pain, no spreading redness/systemic features, normal ROM, clinician’s low concern.

- Issue 1: Left olecranon bursitis (likely aseptic)
  - Plan:
    - Start ibuprofen 400 mg PO twice daily after food; discontinue if heartburn occurs. No duration specified.
    - Proceed with ordered blood tests (inflammatory markers, infection screen, rheumatologic antibodies, serum urate).
    - Follow-up after test results (clinic visit, video, or phone per patient preference).

- Issue 2: Rule out gout/crystal arthropathy
  - Plan:
    - Serum urate as part of labs; review results at follow-up and adjust management accordingly.

- Issue 3: Rule out infection (septic arthritis/bursitis)
  - Plan:
    - Safety-net: Seek urgent assessment if elbow becomes very red, very painful, or if redness spreads/worsens; this would be an emergency requiring immediate evaluation.

- General plan items:
  - Blood test forms to be mailed; patient to complete tests promptly.
  - Results expected ~5–6 days post–blood draw; patient to contact the clinic afterward to arrange review.
  - Follow-up can be remote or face-to-face based on convenience and symptom progression.

Quality checks:
- Missing elements: Vitals not recorded; comprehensive ROS limited; smoking/alcohol history not recorded; medication start date/duration not specified.
- Conflicts: Patient states DOB 04/05/1973 and also reports age as 53 (conflict noted).
- Transcript quality: Clear; video exam limited to visual inspection and patient-reported palpation.
